query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High‐throughput computational screening, when integrated with controlled melting and heat‐treatment protocols, can be used to achieve phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization in high‐entropy alloys by guiding the formation of beneficial nanoscale precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: A candidate high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system) produced by conventional arc-melting without targeted composition tuning.
generation.intervention: Apply high‐throughput computational screening to identify optimal compositions followed by experimental processing that includes repeated arc-melting for homogeneity, drop-casting, homogenization at high temperature, and controlled annealing.
generation.conditions: Processing conditions that ensure full mixing (multiple remelts), homogenization at around 1200 °C, and subsequent annealing near 700 °C for a short duration; composition range roughly with Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.%.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale L21 precipitates (or, depending on slight composition deviations, ordered antiphase domains) within a BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The computationally guided composition selection promotes the formation of a load-bearing, thermodynamically stable ordered phase (nanoscale L21 precipitates) that refines the microstructure and enhances precipitation strengthening through load-transfer effects, thereby improving yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally processed alloy without compositional optimization, the high‐throughput designed alloy will display a more refined microstructure (with precipitate sizes on the order of 10–30 nm), higher volume fraction of the strengthening phase, and superior high-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., improved yield strength, potentially exceeding 1000 MPa at 600 °C).
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys produced via conventional methods lacking computationally informed compositional tuning tend to have coarser precipitate structures and lower high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective in the studied compositional range (e.g., Al < 25 at.%, Mn > 15 at.%) and under processing conditions that allow for sufficient homogenization and precise annealing, while applicability outside these limits remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative magnitude of the improvements in yield strength and the exact processing windows needed to reproducibly obtain the optimal precipitate morphology; additional work is needed to refine the phase diagram and thermodynamic database for such alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of a selected Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti high‐entropy alloy sample: one using conventional composition selection and processing, and a second using high‐throughput computational screening to optimize composition followed by the same processing (arc-melting, homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for fixed durations). Ensure other processing variables are kept constant.
measurements: Determine phase constitution using XRD and TEM to ascertain the presence-volume fraction and size of L21 precipitates or equivalent ordered phases.
Conduct mechanical testing (e.g., compression or tensile tests) at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–700 °C) to measure yield strength and other mechanical properties.
Perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM) to measure grain and precipitate sizes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high‐throughput computationally optimized alloy does not exhibit significantly finer precipitate structures (e.g., precipitate size not reduced to the nanoscale range, or similar volume fraction and morphology) and does not outperform the baseline (conventionally processed) alloy in high-temperature mechanical properties (yield strength comparable to or lower than the baseline), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
